    Changelog

    Source: NEWS.md

    harbouR 0.1.0

    First release.

    • Joins return their values. A SeaTable 6.2 server keys the cells of an implicit join (FROM a, b WHERE ...) by their place in the select list - "0000", "0001" - so every value of a join came back NA from hb_query() and the explorer’s Query panel, with the right number of rows. Such a reply is now read by position.

    • Writing back a view read no longer erases the columns it hides. hb_read_table(view = ) returns those columns as NA, and hb_update_rows() sent the NAs back, which cleared the cells on the server. A cell of such a column is now left out of the write unless it has been filled in, and the warning on reading says so.

    • hb_add_select_option() adds the option. A SeaTable 6.2 server refuses an option that lacks either colour, so every call failed with “options invalid”. Options are now sent with an amber colour and dark text, and hb_dtable() gives its options a text colour too.

    • NA in a list column is stored as an empty cell. Taken from an ordinary vector, NA went out as [null] for geolocation, collaborator, image, multiple-select and file columns, and the server stored it so. A [null] geolocation then read back as list(list(NULL)) and stopped every export of the base - hb_dtable(), hb_write_csv(), hb_write_xlsx() and all three downloads of the explorer - with “values must be length 1”. Such NAs are now sent as an empty cell, a stored [null] reads as one, and the flattening of cells for CSV and Excel copes with a missing or repeated field.

    • Date-times in a server’s .dtable export read at the right time. A server stores a date-time as the time it shows, in its own zone, with no offset, and its export keeps it so; harbouR read it as UTC, an hour or two off for a server in Europe, so the same table read differently from the file and from the server. Name the server’s zone with options(harbouR.dtable_tz = "Europe/Berlin"); unset, such values are read as UTC with a warning once a session. hb_dtable() now writes a date-time with its offset, which the server stores as the instant whatever zone it runs in, and a Date column - or one holding only midnights UTC, as hb_read_table() reads a date-only column - as a date column rather than a date-time one.

    • A write is no longer sent twice after a server error. Every request was retried after a 500, 502, 503 or 504, so an append that a proxy gave up on after the server had applied it could store its rows twice. POST, PUT and DELETE requests are now retried only after a 429, which means the server declined them; GET requests keep their retries. hb_query() sends all SQL as POST, so a SELECT that meets a 5xx now fails at once as well.

    • A base token is renewed before it lapses. The API gateway refuses an expired base token with HTTP 403 “invalid token”, and harbouR renewed it only after a 401, so a client older than the token’s three days failed every base call with harbour_error_permission. The token is now renewed a few minutes before the expiry it carries, and once more after a 403 “invalid token”; any other 403 is still not retried. Should the early renewal fail for a moment, the call goes ahead with the token that is still valid. hb_check_credentials() on a username/password client also drops the cached base token once the login succeeds.

    • Date-only cells read from a server no longer land on the day before. SeaTable sends such a cell as midnight in the server’s time zone, with its offset (2030-06-20T00:00:00+02:00), and harbouR converted that instant to UTC, so on any server east of UTC hb_read_table(), hb_get_row() and hb_query() returned the evening before. A date column whose format has no time now reads as midnight UTC on the date SeaTable shows, and is written as YYYY-MM-DD, so reading a cell and writing it back keeps its day on either side of UTC. A date-time written to such a column is sent as the date it shows in its own time zone, except one at exactly midnight UTC, which keeps its UTC date. Date-time cells, dates stored without an offset (as in a .dtable) and columns that report no format read as before.

    • Security:

      • hb_read_dtable(assets = "extract") extracted whatever names an archive held, so a crafted .dtable - the explorer opens uploads this way - could write files outside assets_dir, ~/.Rprofile among them. An archive whose asset entries are absolute, climb out with .. or are symbolic links is now refused before anything is extracted, and only entries under asset/ count as assets.
      • A content.json, or a server’s reply, that is a short string rather than JSON is no longer read as a file path or fetched as a URL, which jsonlite::fromJSON() does with such a string. It is parsed as JSON text only.
      • print() on a client ran any {...} in the base name or server URL as R code, and so did hb_write_dtable() with a table name when it refused a base. Both now show the text as it is.
      • The error from a request that got no answer held the client’s API token, password and cached tokens, so saving it - with saveRDS(), or by returning it from a parallel worker - wrote them out. It no longer holds them, nor the request httr2 chains under it: its body, the rows of a write among them, and with httr2 before 1.2.0 its Authorization header in clear text. A malformed api_token or password is no longer shown in hb_client()’s error message.
      • Requests no longer follow redirects. curl drops the Authorization header when a redirect changes host, port or scheme, so a server given as http:// that redirects to https:// made a good token look refused. A redirect is now an error that says where it points.
      • hb_read_dtable() refuses a file that would unpack to more than options(harbouR.max_dtable_bytes), 4 GiB by default, before reading it: a few megabytes of compressed text unpacked to gigabytes in memory, and the explorer accepts uploads of 1 GB. It refuses an assets_dir that already holds an asset tree, which the next hb_write_dtable() would have packed into this base’s file.
      • An archive written over a file only its owner may read was readable by others for as long as it took to write.

    • Errors:

      • Credentials the server refuses raise harbour_error_auth, as hb_check_credentials() documents. A wrong password (HTTP 400) raised harbour_error_http with “SeaTable returned an error.”, and an unknown API token (HTTP 403) harbour_error_permission. The old class is kept alongside, and the message passes on the server’s reason.
      • A request that gets no answer - a refused connection, a DNS or TLS failure, a timeout, a dropped connection - raises harbour_error_http with status NA and the request’s URL from every function, hb_ping() included. It escaped as httr2’s bare httr2_failure; that class is kept, so handlers written for it still match. The message says the server could not be reached only when nothing was sent - hb_ping() keeps its own words - and after a timeout, a request that can change data says to check before sending it again, since the server may have applied it.
      • ?"harbouR-conditions" now lists the warning classes, and says that argument-matching errors from rlang keep the classes rlang gives them.
      • hb_ping() reported every failure as “Could not reach”, a 404 from a wrong path or a 429 included; an answer that was an error now keeps its own class. A reply that is not JSON, whatever its status, keeps its URL and the start of its text on the error.
      • A 429 whose Retry-After asks for more than a minute is reported at once: httr2 waits as long as the header says, so one asking for an hour blocked the session for an hour per retry.
      • A name or id of one or two dots is refused before anything is sent: curl resolves such a path segment away, so hb_get_view(, ".") listed the views.

    • Reading from a server:

      • hb_query() returned every column of a join as NA: SeaTable keys the cells of a join by column key whatever convert_keys says, and a 6.2 server by position. Both are now read, under the names the server reports.
      • A column added or renamed by someone else since the metadata was cached was left out of hb_read_table() and hb_get_row(), its values dropped. A row that names a column the cache does not know now fetches the metadata again, once.
      • An empty cell reads as NA whichever way the base is read: the API leaves it out of the row, while a .dtable stores "". A select cell whose option has since been deleted reads as NA from a file, as it does from the server, rather than as the option’s id.
      • Geolocation fields read in one order, lng then lat; the list and get-row endpoints send them in different orders, so the same cell read two ways was not identical().
      • A number read into a text column - a formula’s result, say - is written in full, "15000000000" rather than "1.5e+10", and an array result keeps every element instead of its first.
      • hb_query() no longer warns about a missing LIMIT for a statement that is not a SELECT.
      • hb_read_table() through a view returns the columns the view hides as NA, because SeaTable leaves them out of the rows. That looked like empty data; it now warns, naming them.
      • hb_read_table() gave up after 1000 requests whatever their size, so with a small page_size a large table was an error, and so was one ending exactly on the limit. The limit is now about ten million rows, a read that ends on it completes, and a server that returns the same page twice is stopped at once.
      • hb_query()’s warning about a missing LIMIT came at most once every eight hours across all queries, so later ones were cut to 100 rows without a word, and the word limit anywhere in the SQL silenced it. It is now rate-limited per query and ignores quoted strings and back-ticked names.
      • Reading a table whose date cells repeat is faster: each distinct date string in a column is parsed once, and pages are combined once at the end rather than on every request.

    • Writing to a server:

      • A checkbox is sent as a JSON boolean. A 0/1 column, which is how read.csv() and most exports store a flag, went out as numbers, which SeaTable stores as unticked. A number is ticked unless it is 0, and a string is read as as.logical() reads it ("TRUE", "true" or "T", and the same for FALSE); any other string is sent as empty, with a warning, rather than guessed.
      • The file object hb_upload_file() returns, written as tibble(Reports = list(obj)), went out as an array of its fields; it is now the array of objects a file cell holds. A named vector of image URLs, one hidden_columns key in hb_update_view(), named row ids in hb_lock_rows() and hb_unlock_rows(), and named parameters in hb_query() all went out as JSON objects or strings rather than arrays.
      • Inf, -Inf and NaN, which JSON cannot hold, are still sent as null, but now with one warning per write naming the columns. In a checkbox column a number ticks the box unless it is 0, so Inf and -Inf tick it, and NaN is sent empty without a warning. A difftime written to a duration column is sent in seconds, the unit SeaTable stores; 90 minutes went out as 90. hb_update_rows() now serialises through the same path as hb_append_rows().
      • hb_update_column() with only column_data named the type from the cached schema, so a column whose type had changed since was converted back. It now asks the server.
      • A POSIXlt written to a date-time column was sent as its wall-clock time labelled as UTC; it is now sent as the instant it stands for.
      • hb_add_columns() lost a formula column without a word: SeaTable’s batch endpoint answers 200 and does not create it. Every column the reply leaves out is now created on its own.
      • A number written to a text column is sent as text, so an integer64 key past 2^53 keeps its digits rather than being rounded by the server. A row with no cell to write is sent as an object rather than [].
      • A view whose name holds a slash, or is one or two dots, cannot be addressed by name: SeaTable’s proxy decodes the escaped slash. Such a view is found in the table’s list of views by hb_get_view(), and hb_update_view() and hb_delete_view() refuse it, saying why, before sending anything; the server’s 404 blamed the base.

    • Files:

      • hb_download_file() recognised an asset URL only when it began with the client’s server exactly as typed. A relative URL, the form SeaTable writes into cells, failed, and a host in other capitals, http for https or an explicit :443 was fetched directly, saving SeaTable’s login page as the file. Asset URLs are now recognised by their path, and a download that ends on the login page fails.
      • The download and delete endpoints act on the client’s base whatever a URL names, so a URL from another base downloaded, or deleted, this base’s file at the same path. hb_download_file() and hb_delete_asset() now refuse a URL of another base or server, and hb_delete_asset() refuses one that names no file - the server itself, an asset URL cut short, or a path with . or .. in it - instead of asking to delete the asset root or a folder.
      • hb_upload_file() escapes the folders of a custom relative_path like the file name, and its file object has the type "file", as SeaTable’s own file cells do, rather than a MIME type. Its help says what the default relative_path = "files" stands for.
      • On a server reached under a path, such as https://example.org/seatable, download and delete sent that path as part of the asset’s, so harbouR could not fetch or remove a file it had uploaded itself.
      • The client’s timeout cut a download off after 30 seconds however fast it arrived, and an upload had no limit at all. Both are now limited to that long connecting, and a download to that long without moving data. An upload folder that climbs out with .. is refused.

    • The client:

      • Logging in and exchanging an API token work for a server reached under a path, such as https://example.org/seatable; both went to the root of the host.
      • hb_client() refuses a workspace_id, base_name or timeout that could not work, instead of failing at the first request, and sends a round workspace id such as 1e5 as 100000 rather than 1e+05. A username/password client remembers the base it named, so hb_metadata()$base_name is its name rather than NA.
      • A username/password client no longer reads SEATABLE_API_TOKEN: with the variable set, as the README suggests, it was refused for holding both kinds of credentials.
      • timeout = Inf sets no limit; it was accepted, then every request failed with a curl error of no harbouR class. A finite timeout curl cannot take is refused. base_uuid is checked, and escaped in the URL.
      • hb_check_credentials() keeps the base token it has when the check fails for a moment, instead of leaving the client without one.

    • .dtable files:

      • hb_read_dtable(assets = "extract") extracted only one of two attachments whose names differ only in case, on any system, since zip::unzip() finds an entry without regard to case; writing the base back then lost the other without a word. It now warns, naming them, and the explorer shows that warning when it opens such a file.
      • In R 4.1 and 4.2, the _ctime and _mtime of a base built by hb_dtable(), hb_read_csv(), hb_read_xlsx() or the explorer were the local time labelled as UTC. They are now UTC there as well.
      • hb_write_dtable() builds the archive beside its destination and moves it into place once complete, so a failed write cannot destroy the file it replaces, even the one the base was read from. The bytes written are the same. A destination that cannot be replaced - another program holds it open, or the folder lets files be written but not removed - is written into once the archive is complete, and should that fail, the complete archive is kept beside it and the error says where. An asset that cannot be copied stops the write, and links in the asset tree are left out, with a warning, instead of followed.
      • Text in a .dtable read in a session that is not UTF-8 - Rscript under cron, or a container with LANG unset - came back mangled, and hb_write_dtable() then saved it that way. It now reads as it does in a UTF-8 session.
      • print() and the warning about assets that will not be written counted the archive’s folders as assets: the example showed 7 for its 2 files.
      • On a .dtable, hb_read_table(view = ) applies none of the view’s filters or sorts, which its help now says; a filtered view that records no rows warns that every row was returned.
      • hb_dtable() drops a column named _id, such as the one hb_read_table() adds: kept, it became a column SeaTable imported and harbouR then refused to read. hb_validate_dtable() reports a table or row without an _id, a column without a key, type or name, a column named _id, and empty view settings.
      • hb_asset_path() resolves the escaped URLs of SeaTable’s own export: an attachment whose name holds a space, an umlaut or a bracket gave NA.
      • Attachments whose names are not ASCII extract in a C locale; the read failed with an error of no harbouR class.
      • A NUL character in content.json, which R cannot keep, and object keys JSON cannot keep - empty or repeated - are reported instead of changing quietly.

    • CSV and Excel:

      • In R before 4.4.1, hb_read_csv() read a code such as 12E as the number 12, as read.csv() does there. A column holding one now stays text, as it does in later versions of R.
      • In a UTF-8 session, a zero-padded or long integer followed by a full-width or other Unicode space, which read.csv() ignores after a number, became a number: "0001" padded that way read as 1. Such a column now stays text, like one padded with an ordinary space.
      • Re-importing an export gave a base none of whose tables could be read: the exported _id became an ordinary column. hb_read_csv() and hb_read_xlsx() now drop a column of that name, which SeaTable keeps for its row identifier; one that holds anything but SeaTable row ids - a database’s keys, say - is dropped with a warning naming its table.
      • hb_read_csv() kept read.csv()’s type guessing, which ignores quoting, so "0001" came back as 1 - the auto-number column of an export among them - and a 19-digit barcode was rounded. A column holding an integer with a leading zero, or one of more than 15 digits, now stays text; every other column is typed as before. The help now says that dates arrive as text and that a literal NA is read as missing.
      • hb_read_csv() refuses a file whose bytes are not valid UTF-8, naming the line; a Windows-1252 file, as Excel’s plain “CSV” often is, was cut off at its first accented letter. In a session that is not UTF-8, a valid UTF-8 file was cut off at the first character the session could not hold, and one with a byte-order mark failed; hb_write_csv() there wrote such characters as text like <U+00B0>. Both now read and write UTF-8 in a single-byte session such as C or Latin-1; a multibyte one, such as Shift-JIS, converts the text into its own encoding as before. An empty file is refused, naming it, and an empty column is text rather than a checkbox reading FALSE in every row.
      • hb_read_xlsx() judges a column’s type by every row of the sheet. readxl looked at the first 1000, and later values that did not fit were lost.
      • A file or sheet named collaborators or base_name imports as a table; the first used to vanish into the base’s collaborator list. hb_write_xlsx() refuses table names that differ only in case, or that clash once shortened and cleaned to Excel’s rules, which Excel cannot hold as separate sheets. The flattening message names every column instead of the first 20, and the help lists every loss the exports make.
      • CSV file names keep their letters: every character outside A to Z became _, so two tables named in Chinese both became _.csv and the export was refused, and Probenübersicht re-imported as Proben_bersicht. Only what a file name cannot hold is replaced.
      • harbouR makes sheet names legal for Excel itself, so writexl before 2.0.0 no longer fails on a table name holding / or ?. Text longer than the 32,767 characters a workbook cell holds is refused, naming its column, instead of failing inside libxlsxwriter.
      • hb_read_xlsx() keeps the spaces around text, which readxl stripped from values, and hb_read_csv() keeps a column text when it holds a telephone number with a leading plus; a signed number such as +1.5 is still a number.

    • The explorer:

      • hb_run_explorer() used a compact symbol in its header; it now shows the named v5 artwork. Missing packaged artwork raises harbour_error_package_asset and identifies the missing file.
      • hb_run_explorer() needs bslib 0.6.0 or later, now the minimum that DESCRIPTION lists. An older one gets the same informative error as a missing one, instead of a stack trace.
      • What opening a file warns about - attachments that cannot all be extracted, a newer .dtable format - is shown in the app; it reached only the R console.
      • “This table as CSV” held only the rows the Data panel had loaded, 1000 by default; it now holds the whole table. The zipped CSV left out any table whose name starts with a dot.
      • The Export panel said a .dtable keeps everything. For a live base that file is rebuilt from the rows, so column types are inferred again and select options, attachments and views are lost; for a file opened without its assets, the attachments are left out. The panel now says which applies, and a live base’s .dtable download shows a notification. That download also kept a table named collaborators out of the file, and failed on one named base_name.
      • A failed download is reported in the app rather than only in the R console, and a missing writexl is named instead of prompting at the console. The Query panel says, on every query without LIMIT, that SeaTable returned at most 100 rows. The app accepts uploads up to 1 GB while it runs, unless shiny.maxRequestSize is set: the 5 MB that Shiny allows by default refused most real exports.
      • The source badge was dark text on a translucent tint over the dark masthead, and the muted grey fell just short of 4.5:1; both now read. The SQL box has a label.
      • A statement other than SELECT showed reactable’s own error and a notice about a LIMIT it does not take; the panel now says the statement ran, and that such statements change the base.
      • Opening the example base is handled like every other action, so a failure is reported instead of ending the session. The attachments the app unpacks are removed when another base is opened and when the session ends; those of each upload stayed until R quit.
      • The help for host says what a reachable explorer gives away: it has no login.

    • Documentation and tests:

      • The live tests cover the server contracts the mocked tests cannot see - joins, select options, writing back a view read, NA in list columns, formula columns added in a batch, and date-time round trips. Five of the six failed against a SeaTable 6.2.1 server before these fixes, while every mocked test passed.

      • The spelling test can fail; it reported its findings and passed. DT, dplyr and ggplot2, suggested but used nowhere, are no longer listed. The README no longer says that everything works offline, and the help says what hb_list_columns()$editable and hb_append_rows()$n_rows mean.

      • README and vignette pages used different logos; they now use standardised named v5 artwork in matching light and dark forms.

      • The examples that need a server are wrapped in \dontrun{}. They ran whenever R was interactive, so example() sent their writes and deletes to the base that SEATABLE_SERVER and SEATABLE_API_TOKEN name. hb_read_table(), hb_list_tables(), hb_list_columns(), hb_list_views(), hb_client(), the is_harbour_*() predicates and the harbour_metadata methods gain examples that run offline. The hb_create_table() example names columns, which it passed into ...; the hb_metadata() example calls tibble::as_tibble(); and the conditions example no longer depends on the caller’s token.

      • The help pages of hb_read_table(), hb_list_tables() and hb_list_views() are named after the function rather than its .dtable method. ?harbouR no longer shows stray backslashes, the Get-started vignette no longer refers to a NOTICE.md the package does not ship, and the arguments of hb_update_select_option(), hb_delete_select_option(), hb_lock_rows(), hb_unlock_rows() and hb_update_view() say what those functions do with them. The help of the print(), format(), summary() and as_tibble() methods no longer calls their ... unused: it must be empty.

      • The explorer’s tests no longer leave sass’s cache of compiled CSS in the home directory, and the test that renders a request with httr2::req_dry_run() skips on CRAN and without httpuv.

      • The tests need testthat 3.2.0 or later, now the minimum that DESCRIPTION lists.

      • The API lock pins the signatures of the registered S3 methods as well as the exports: the arguments users pass to hb_read_table() and the hb_list_*() verbs belong to the methods, not the generics, so a changed default there passed the lock. The new section matches the manuscript anchor exactly.

      • Golden tests pin what the offline paths return: every column of the bundled example as read, hb_column_types(), the example data, the .dtable and CSV files the writers produce, and what the CSV and Excel exports read back as.

      • pkgdown builds the citation page from the source DESCRIPTION, so it cited the maintainer alone; it now lists all six authors.

      • hb_column_types() corrects three notes: single-select values are not validated on write (SeaTable adds an unknown name as a new option), an unset checkbox reads as FALSE, and digital-signature cells are left out of writes because a signature should come from the signer. Its help says percent, dollar and euro are number formats, which SeaTable reports as type number, rather than column types.

      • The examples and README read the example file with assets = "extract" before writing it back, the hb_asset_path() example resolves a file the example holds, and hb_dtable()‘s help notes that building a base advances .Random.seed. The help no longer says hb_append_rows()’s reply lacks the new rows’ ids, nor that the example rows cover every column type.

      • The explorer’s tests skip rather than error without readxl, shiny or htmltools, and two static checks that skipped in every CI job now run there. The live-server tests compare harbouR’s reads with what the server sent, and delete only the row they created.

    • Audited the server wrappers against SeaTable’s published OpenAPI specification (v6.2) and the server responses recorded in its test suite. The mocked tests could only prove that harbouR built the request it intended; several of those requests were not the ones the server expects:

      • hb_read_table() and hb_get_row() now send convert_keys=true. The server’s default keys every cell by column key, so a live read came back with every column NA.
      • hb_create_view(), hb_get_view(), hb_update_view() and hb_delete_view() name the table in the query string, where the server reads it, rather than in the body. hb_list_views() and hb_get_view() recognise the default view by its id, because the server reports no is_default.
      • hb_upload_file(), hb_delete_asset() and hb_download_file() authenticate with the API token, as SeaTable’s file endpoints require, instead of a base token. hb_download_file() exchanges an asset URL for a download link first - fetching a cell’s URL directly saved SeaTable’s login page - and writes through a temporary file, so a failed download leaves nothing behind and does not destroy the file it was asked to replace.
      • hb_attach_file() writes the shape each column holds: a file object, wrapped in the array a file cell is, or the URL for an image column. It refuses other column types.
      • hb_add_columns() accepts name/type specs like hb_create_table(); they were sent verbatim, with field names the server does not read. hb_update_column() with only column_data names the column’s current type, which the server requires.

    • Every HTTP error whose body parsed as JSON - most of them - crashed with “Can’t supply conflicting bodies” from rlang::abort() instead of raising a harbour_error, because the body was stored in the field abort() reserves for its own use. It is now response_body. The server’s message is shown whether it arrives as error_msg, error_message or plain text. The test fixture could not be parsed, which is how this went unnoticed.

    • A missing number in hb_append_rows() or hb_update_rows() was sent as the string "NA"; it is now null.

    • Geolocation and digital-signature cells keep their field names when read, and geolocation cells are written back as objects. Unnamed, a location read as list(50, 8.23) and was written as [50, 8.23].

    • An empty multiple-select cell read from a .dtable is character(0), matching a populated one; it was logical(0).

    • hb_dtable() stores select cells as option ids, as SeaTable’s own files do, and creates options for multiple-select columns. Cells held option names, which harbouR read back correctly but SeaTable showed as empty. List-columns of objects are flattened to text rather than becoming nonsense select options.

    • hb_append_rows() warns about columns the table does not have, which it drops; it used to drop them silently. Row-id verbs refuse missing or empty ids, and hb_query(convert_keys = FALSE) reads cells by key.

    • Final minor refinements: constrain bundled asset paths to their extraction directory and reject colliding CSV filenames before writing files.

    • Exclude local administration and repository citation metadata from source builds, and use the repository citation URL until the archival record is publicly available.

    harbouR is an unofficial R client for the SeaTable REST API. It connects to a SeaTable server, reads and writes rows as tidy tibbles, manages tables, columns and views, uploads and attaches files, reads and writes local .dtable exports with no server at all, and ships a Shiny explorer for doing all of that without writing code.

    The notes below record what changed during development, against an 0.1.0 that was tagged but never published.

    • The maintainer address is now raban.heller@uni-ulm.de, and URL / BugReports point at https://github.com/CTTIR/harbouR, which is where the package actually lives. Paul Elsinghorst, Wiebke Derz, Matthias Ring, Gerhard Achatz and Vinzent Forstmeier are credited as contributors.

    • hb_example_metadata() now reads the demo base from inst/extdata/example_metadata.json rather than duplicating it in R source, so there is a single definition to maintain.

    • HTTP 404 responses now name the failing endpoint instead of erroring while trying to format the message.

    • httptest2 has been dropped from Suggests: it was never used, and its absence turned R CMD check red on any machine without it. HTTP is replaced at the package’s own request seam instead.

    • Errors now carry condition classes under a shared harbour_error, so they can be caught by kind rather than by message text. See ?"harbouR-conditions". HTTP errors carry status, url and response_body.

    • A 403 response is no longer retried as though the base token had expired. A 401 triggers a refresh, and so does a 403 that says the token itself is invalid.

    • hb_ping() and hb_server_info() no longer send an Authorization header. Both endpoints are unauthenticated, and demanding an API token made them fail for username/password clients - exactly the case where checking connectivity matters most.

    • hb_ping() now returns the client invisibly rather than TRUE, so it composes: client |> hb_ping() |> hb_read_table("Samples"). New hb_check_credentials() covers the other half of the old behaviour - proving the credentials are accepted, not just that the server is up.

    • Reading a table whose schema contains a column literally named _id now errors with a harbour_error_column_collision condition instead of silently overwriting it with the SeaTable row identifier.

    • hb_run_explorer() restores the previous value of the harbouR_preset_client Shiny option when it exits. A client carrying a plaintext token used to stay reachable in process-global state for the rest of the session.

    • Every base-scoped request now addresses a real resource. The base UUID was captured from the token exchange and then never interpolated into a URL, so all 24 base-scoped paths pointed at a collection with no base identifier. hb_metadata() additionally used a service prefix, /dtables/api/v1/, that does not exist - and because every other function lazily depends on it, its failure cascaded to all of them.

    • harbouR now targets the SeaTable API gateway. /dtable-server/ and /dtable-db/ were deprecated in SeaTable 5.2 and removed in 5.3; harbouR addressed them exclusively. Base operations move to /api-gateway/api/v2/dtables/{base_uuid}/, which also collapses the three-host service switch to one. Base tokens are sent as Bearer, which is what the gateway expects; the web API keeps Token. This requires SeaTable 5.3 (June 2025) or newer.

    Legal position

    • NOTICE.md, the README, the vignette and ?harbouR now cite the basis on which harbouR uses SeaTable’s interface, rather than implying it rests on a licence grant. Endpoint paths, HTTP verbs and JSON field names are the ideas and principles underlying an interface, excluded from copyright protection by Article 1(2) of Directive 2009/24/EC and by the CJEU in SAS Institute v World Programming (C-406/10) - which was referred, on these facts, the question whether a program may be written to read and write another’s data file format.

    • They also cite the clause in SeaTable’s own dtable-server EULA that defines applications communicating over the API as “third-party software” and states that the EULA’s provisions “do not apply to any such third-party software”.

    • Two factual corrections: the per-component licences previously attributed to SeaTable Server could not be verified from the repositories, and the API specification is published publicly but is not openly licensed. Both statements are gone. The one verbatim quotation in the package is now attributed to its source.

    • The wording is deliberately narrow. harbouR relies on the interface exclusion rather than asserting that it settles the question, because it does not settle everything: the CJEU reserved the possibility that a data file format could attract ordinary copyright as a work (C-406/10, para. 45), and § 69g(1) UrhG leaves unfair competition, trade secrets, trademarks and contract untouched. Both limits are stated in NOTICE.md, along with the fact that none of this is legal advice.

    Scope

    • harbouR is stated, throughout, as being for two things: SeaTable .dtable data files, read and written directly with no server; and a SeaTable Server you run yourself, over its REST API. The Title and Description say so, and there is a “What harbouR is for” section in the README and in ?harbouR.

    • The explorer’s server field no longer pre-fills a vendor-hosted address; it is empty, with a neutral placeholder, unless SEATABLE_SERVER is set. The documented examples for hb_client() and for the live tests use a self-hosted URL.

    • Nothing here restricts where you point the package. hb_client() takes a server URL as an argument and makes no judgement about the host; the scope statement describes what harbouR is built and documented for, not what it will refuse to do.

    Acknowledgement

    • New Acknowledgements section in the README, the introductory vignette and ?harbouR, naming what SeaTable GmbH and Seafile Ltd. built that made an independent client possible: a publicly published OpenAPI specification kept per server version, a reference readable without an account, manuals in repositories that accept pull requests, Apache-2.0 client libraries, a Developer Edition you can host yourself - and a changelog that records removals as plainly as additions. That last one is not abstract: it is how harbouR learned it had been aimed at endpoints removed in SeaTable 5.3.

      The section is careful about what it does and does not claim: SeaTable Server is not open source, and it says so. A later adversarial review found two assertions in the first version of this text that were not in fact supported by their sources - the per-component licences of SeaTable Server, and the claim that the API specification is “openly licensed” - and both have been corrected. harbouR needs no licence to the specification: endpoint paths, verbs and field names are excluded from copyright protection as the ideas underlying an interface.

    Authorship and citation

    • Paul Elsinghorst, Wiebke Derz, Matthias Ring, Gerhard Achatz and Vinzent Forstmeier are credited as authors (aut), not contributors.

    • New inst/CITATION, so citation("harbouR") produces a proper reference and BibTeX entry naming every author. It reads the package’s own metadata, so the authors, version and year cannot drift out of step with DESCRIPTION. README and the introductory vignette both carry a Citation section.

    Fixes from the post-rewrite audit

    • Security: the explorer’s Schema tab rendered a column’s type string as raw HTML. A .dtable carrying a crafted type could run script in a session that may hold the user’s API token. The type is now escaped.

    • Data loss: hb_write_dtable() dropped the bundled asset/ tree unless the base had been read with assets = "extract", producing an archive whose attachment cells pointed at files it did not contain. The explorer now extracts on open, and the writer warns rather than discarding silently.

    • Exporting a live base to .dtable wrote _id as an ordinary column, which then collided with the reserved name on read - the export could not be re-opened. System fields are dropped first.

    • hb_update_rows() threw a bare “subscript out of bounds” for any column not in the table’s schema, which is what hb_read_table() |> mutate() |> hb_update_rows() produces. It now names the offending column. It also drops server-computed columns, which hb_append_rows() already did.

    • hb_duplicate_table() sent an undocumented new_table_name and omitted the required is_duplicate_records. It gains duplicate_records and documents that SeaTable always names the copy <original>(copy), with no space.

    • hb_create_table() documented column specs as name/type while the API wants column_name/column_type, so following the package’s own example produced a body the server rejects. Both spellings now work.

    • hb_client() and hb_read_dtable() validate their arguments before using them, so a wrong type gives a classed harbouR error rather than a raw R one.

    • Writing Inf to a .dtable warns. JSON cannot hold it, so it becomes null and reads back as NA; that is now visible. NaN is written as an empty cell, as NA is.

    • The endpoint contract test pins request-body field names as well as paths. Renaming a body field previously left the suite green.

    The explorer

    • The Shiny app has been rebuilt, and it lives in R/. It was under inst/, where R CMD check, covr and lintr could not see it - which is how it came to use an operator that does not exist on three of the four R versions the package claims to support. Its logic is now driven headlessly by shiny::testServer() in the test suite, and codecov.yml no longer hides it from the coverage number.

    • hb_run_explorer() opens a local .dtable, connects to a server, or loads a bundled example base that needs no credentials and no network. Its first argument takes either a harbour_client or a harbour_dtable.

    • Everything is reachable without code: browse tables, read the schema, run SQL, and download the base as .dtable, Excel or zipped CSV - or the open table as a single CSV.

    • The palette is the package logo’s, which is viridis. Column types are grouped into families, each keeping one colour throughout, and every table in the sidebar carries a band showing its columns by family - so the shape of a sixty-column table is legible before you open it.

    • The API token field is never pre-filled from the environment. A value passed to a password input is serialised into the page’s HTML.

    Local .dtable files

    • harbouR reads and writes SeaTable .dtable exports. hb_read_dtable() opens one; hb_write_dtable() writes it back. Round-tripping is lossless, verified against a real 750 KB export: read then write then read yields an identical structure, including fields harbouR does not model.

    • The same verbs work on a file as on a live base. hb_list_tables(), hb_list_columns(), hb_list_views() and hb_read_table() are now S3 generics with harbour_client and harbour_dtable methods, so an analysis can be written once and run either way. Their first argument is named x; the write verbs keep client, because they need a server.

    • hb_dtable() builds a base from R data frames, inferring column types, so a set of tables can be written out and imported into SeaTable. hb_validate_dtable() reports what would stop a base importing, and the writer refuses to produce a file that would fail.

    • hb_write_xlsx() and hb_write_csv() export to spreadsheets, naming exactly which columns had to be flattened; hb_read_xlsx() and hb_read_csv() build a new base from them. The lossy direction is documented rather than implied.

    • Select-option ids are translated to their display names, because a file stores the id where the API returns the name - without this a local read and a server read of the same column disagreed.

    • hb_asset_path() resolves a bundled file://dtable-bundle/ URL to a local file when the base was read with assets = "extract".

    The SeaTable API

    • hb_query() types its result from the schema SeaTable returns alongside the rows, which harbouR previously discarded. It inferred types from the values instead, so an all-NULL column came back logical and one stray string turned a numeric column into character - the same query could return different types on different days. hb_query() and hb_read_table() now agree.

    • hb_query() warns when the SQL has no LIMIT clause, because SeaTable applies an implicit LIMIT 100, and gains parameters for ? placeholders and convert_keys.

    • The username/password flow works. hb_client() accepted username and password and documented a three-token model, but every base call then aborted with “not supported” and every web call with “API token required”: such a client could do nothing at all. harbouR now performs the account-token to base-token exchange. Because an account token is scoped to the user rather than to a base, hb_client() gains workspace_id and base_name, and says so if they are missing.

    • Percent-encoded path segments no longer reach the server double-encoded. httr2::req_url_path() escapes what it is given, so an already-escaped %20 became %2520; it also leaves / alone, so a view named a/b would have split into two path segments.

    • Dates parse. _ctime and _mtime come back as full ISO-8601 with a UTC offset - 2025-11-28T14:00:24.395+00:00 - and the parser’s format list covered none of the offset-bearing forms, so every creation and modification time read as NA. It now handles the T separator, fractional seconds and offsets, and honours the offset instead of discarding it.

    • List-columns are type-stable. A multiple-select column yielded a character vector for a populated cell and a list for an empty one, so tidyr::unnest(), purrr::map_chr() and vctrs all failed on a table containing a single blank cell. Empty and populated cells now agree, for all 28 types, and a contract test asserts it type by type.

    • Reading a table with no columns returns a 0-row tibble carrying _id, as documented, rather than a 0x0 tibble.

    • An unrecognised column type reads as text rather than erroring, so a future SeaTable release cannot break a read.

    • long-text cells that arrive as an object rather than a string yield their text instead of a mangled coercion.

    • Reading is roughly 70x faster: the type lookup rebuilt the column-type tibble once per cell. Reading the whole of a real 10-table base went from 27s to 0.4s.

    • Breaking: hb_read_table(limit =) is now page_size =, and there is a new n_max =. The old argument was documented as a page size but was also used as the stop condition, so limit = 5000 returned 1000 rows and stopped - a wrong answer with no warning. page_size is clamped to SeaTable’s 1000-row maximum with a warning, n_max bounds the total, and a runaway server now produces an error rather than an infinite loop.

    • hb_append_rows(), hb_update_rows() and hb_delete_rows() split their work into requests of at most 1000 rows, which is SeaTable’s batch limit. Writing 2500 rows used to send one oversized request. All three gain a chunk_size argument.

    • Breaking: the three write verbs return a one-row summary - table, n_rows, n_requests - instead of fabricated per-row results. hb_append_rows() previously fell back to the request payload, which has no server-assigned _id, while promising server-generated ids in its documentation; hb_update_rows() and hb_delete_rows() returned rep(TRUE, n) without looking at the response at all. n_rows from hb_append_rows() is the count the server confirmed.

    • hb_upload_file() returned url = NA on every call, so the object it produced could never be written into a file cell - which is what hb_attach_file(), the flagship helper, does with it. It now requests ret-json=1 (without it the endpoint replies in plain text, so the response was unparseable), uploads to the image or file tree the server nominates rather than a hard-coded files, and builds the asset URL from the workspace id, base UUID and upload path.

    • hb_delete_asset() targeted /api/v2.1/dtable/asset/ with an API token and a url body. The endpoint is /api/v2.1/dtable/app-asset/, takes the API token, and identifies the asset by a path query parameter.

    • Writing a file, image or geolocation cell no longer corrupts it. The write path flattened every list-valued cell with unlist(), which is right for a multiple-select column but turns a file cell’s {name, size, type, url} object into c("report.pdf", "12345", "application/pdf", "https://..."). Serialisation is now driven by the column type. Flat list-columns are emitted as JSON arrays even when they hold a single value, which previously auto-unboxed to a scalar and changed the cell’s type.

    • hb_update_column() sends the op_type field SeaTable requires; without it the request was rejected. It gains a new_type argument for type changes, and refuses to rename and retype in one call, because SeaTable performs one operation per request.

    • hb_update_select_option() sent option/new_option scalars. The API identifies an option by id, so harbouR now reads the column’s options and resolves the name first. hb_delete_select_option() sends the option_names array the API expects rather than a scalar option.

    • hb_list_columns() and hb_list_views() read the columns/ and views/ endpoints rather than only the cached base metadata, and both gain a refresh argument. hb_list_columns() gains a data list-column carrying each column’s type-specific configuration - the select options, the date format - which is what makes option ids resolvable.

    • hb_get_view() coerces its scalars like every sibling function, and reports is_default and hidden_columns.

    • Table, view and row names are percent-encoded into the path, so a view called Erwartungswerte Toxine 1 or a/b no longer produces a broken or ambiguous URL.

    • hb_duplicate_table() posted to tables/duplicate/; the endpoint is tables/duplicate-table/.

    • hb_list_collaborators() called a web-service path that does not exist. It is a base-scoped endpoint and needs the base token.

    • hb_column_types() is now genuinely the single source of truth for the coercion layer. It gains is_list and read_only logical columns, which the coercion functions derive their type sets from instead of repeating hard-coded vectors, and it covers five names it previously omitted: the types duration and digital-sign, and the number formats percent, dollar and euro.

    • Breaking: hb_list_tables() and as_tibble() on a harbour_metadata no longer return an n_rows column. The metadata endpoint carries no row payloads, so the value was structurally always 0 and told every user their tables were empty.

    • New format() methods for harbour_client and harbour_metadata, so their representation can be captured as a character vector rather than only printed.

    • Breaking: the 39 scaffolded endpoints that only ever raised “not yet implemented” have been removed - hb_list_links(), hb_create_base(), hb_export_table(), the hb_admin_*() and hb_team_*() families, and the rest. They were half the exported surface and none of them worked. The remaining areas are listed under Roadmap in the README.
